title: Churn model bake-off: logistic vs random forest vs gradient boosting
summary: Compare three churn models fairly inside one preprocessing pipeline with stratified cross-validation, tune the winner, spot a leakage trap, and judge the result by retention value in the top decile rather than by AUC alone.
business: A telecom operator's postpaid base loses about 1 in 6 subscribers a year. For its next quarterly campaign the retention team can call **10% of the base (50,000 of 5 lakh subscribers)** and offer a ₹300 bill credit; a saved customer is worth about **₹4,800** in margin over the next year and roughly 30% of called would-be churners stay. The head of retention asks: **which model should rank customers for the call list, how much better is it than a simple logistic regression, and what is the ₹ value of one campaign using it?**

dataset.name: Synthetic postpaid subscriber snapshot (8,000 rows)
dataset.how: Generated in step 1 with `numpy.random.default_rng(99)`: tenure, monthly bill (₹), data usage (GB), call drops, complaints in 90 days, plan, contract type, payment method, region and a churn flag from a non-linear rule (interactions and thresholds that trees can exploit). About 4% of some numeric fields are missing. A leaky column is included on purpose.

steps.title: Generate the subscriber snapshot
steps.detail: Churn here depends on interactions (complaints matter much more for month-to-month customers) and thresholds (a jump after 3 call drops), which tree ensembles can capture and plain logistic regression cannot without hand-made features. We also add `retention_call_logged`, which is filled in *after* a customer calls to cancel: a classic leakage trap.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold, cross_validate, RandomizedSearchCV
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from scipy import stats

pd.set_option("display.width", 160); pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 20)
rng = np.random.default_rng(99)
n = 8000
d = pd.DataFrame({
    "tenure_m": rng.integers(1, 72, n),
    "monthly_bill": np.round(rng.normal(649, 220, n).clip(199, 1999)),
    "data_gb": np.round(rng.gamma(3, 8, n), 1),
    "call_drops": rng.poisson(1.5, n),
    "complaints_90d": rng.poisson(0.4, n),
    "plan": rng.choice(["Basic", "Plus", "Max"], n, p=[0.5, 0.35, 0.15]),
    "contract": rng.choice(["Monthly", "Annual"], n, p=[0.6, 0.4]),
    "payment": rng.choice(["Autopay", "UPI", "Cash"], n, p=[0.45, 0.4, 0.15]),
    "region": rng.choice(["North", "South", "East", "West"], n),
})
monthly = d["contract"] == "Monthly"
z = (-2.0 + 0.6 * monthly - 0.02 * d["tenure_m"] + 1.6 * (d["call_drops"] > 3)
     + d["complaints_90d"].clip(0, 3) * np.where(monthly, 1.4, 0.0) + 0.003 * (d["monthly_bill"] - 649).clip(0) * monthly
     + 0.6 * (d["payment"] == "Cash") - 0.8 * (d["data_gb"].between(15, 40)) + 1.5 * ((d["tenure_m"] < 6) & monthly))
d["churn"] = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
d["retention_call_logged"] = ((d["churn"] == 1) & (rng.random(n) < 0.7)) | (rng.random(n) < 0.03)
for c in ["data_gb", "monthly_bill", "call_drops"]:
    d.loc[rng.random(n) < 0.04, c] = np.nan
print(d.head()); print("Churn rate:", round(d["churn"].mean(), 3))

steps.title: Hold out a test set and build one preprocessing block
steps.detail: Split off 20% as a final test set, stratified on churn. Then define preprocessing **once** as a `ColumnTransformer`: median imputation plus scaling for numbers, most-frequent imputation plus one-hot encoding for categories. Putting it inside each model's pipeline means imputation medians are learned only from the training folds during CV, so nothing leaks from validation rows.
steps.code:
features = ["tenure_m", "monthly_bill", "data_gb", "call_drops", "complaints_90d", "plan", "contract", "payment", "region"]
num = features[:5]; cat = features[5:]
train, test = train_test_split(d, test_size=0.2, stratify=d["churn"], random_state=1)
Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte = train[features], train["churn"], test[features], test["churn"]
pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("sc", StandardScaler())]), num),
    ("cat", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")), ("oh", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"))]), cat)])
print(Xtr.isna().mean().round(3)[lambda s: s > 0])

steps.title: Define the three candidate pipelines
steps.detail: Same preprocessing, three learners: regularised **logistic regression** (the transparent baseline), a **random forest** (bagged deep trees, robust, little tuning) and **histogram gradient boosting** (sequential shallow trees, usually strongest on tabular data, very fast). Scaling is irrelevant for trees but harmless, and keeping one preprocessing block keeps the comparison fair.

steps.title: Compare with stratified 5-fold cross-validation
steps.detail: Use the **same** `StratifiedKFold` splits for every model so differences come from the models, not from lucky folds. Score both ROC AUC and average precision (PR AUC), and report mean ± SD across folds. A difference smaller than about one fold-SD is not worth a more complex model.

steps.title: Is the winner really better? Paired fold comparison
steps.detail: Because all models saw identical folds, compare them **pairwise per fold**. The fold-by-fold differences in AUC tell you whether one model wins consistently. A paired t-test on 5 folds is only a rough guide (folds share training data, so it is over-optimistic), but a model that wins on every fold by a clear margin is a safe choice.
steps.code:
diff = scores["grad_boost"]["test_roc_auc"] - scores["logistic"]["test_roc_auc"]
print("GB − logistic AUC per fold:", diff.round(4), "| wins:", int((diff > 0).sum()), "of 5")
print("paired t-test p =", round(stats.ttest_rel(scores["grad_boost"]["test_roc_auc"], scores["logistic"]["test_roc_auc"]).pvalue, 4))

steps.title: Tune gradient boosting with a randomized search
steps.detail: Search learning rate, tree size, number of iterations and L2 regularisation with `RandomizedSearchCV` (12 random combinations, 3-fold CV on the training set only). Randomized search covers wide ranges cheaply. Keep the expectations modest: tuning usually adds a point or two of AUC, much less than good features.
steps.code:
search = RandomizedSearchCV(models["grad_boost"], {
    "m__learning_rate": [0.02, 0.05, 0.1], "m__max_leaf_nodes": [8, 15, 31], "m__max_iter": [150, 300],
    "m__l2_regularization": [0.0, 0.1, 1.0], "m__min_samples_leaf": [20, 50]},
    n_iter=12, cv=StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=0), scoring="roc_auc", random_state=0, n_jobs=-1)
search.fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("Best params:", search.best_params_, "CV AUC", round(search.best_score_, 4))
best = search.best_estimator_

steps.title: Score the test set once and translate into ₹
steps.detail: Refit the baseline and use the tuned model on the full training set, then score the untouched test set. The business metric is the **top decile**: of the 10% of customers the model ranks riskiest, how many actually churn (precision@10%) and what share of all churners that captures. Campaign value ≈ churners reached × 30% save rate × ₹4,800 − calls × ₹300 credit (credit given to everyone called), scaled from the test set to the 5 lakh base. Include the untuned random forest too: if it is within noise of the tuned booster, the simpler-to-tune model may be the better operational choice.
steps.code:
def top_decile(y, p):
    k = int(0.1 * len(y)); idx = np.argsort(-p)[:k]
    return y.to_numpy()[idx].sum(), k
base_n, save, value, credit = 500_000, 0.30, 4800, 300
rows = []
for name, m in {"logistic": models["logistic"].fit(Xtr, ytr), "random_forest": models["random_forest"].fit(Xtr, ytr), "grad_boost_tuned": best}.items():
    p = m.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
    hit, k = top_decile(yte, p)
    scale = base_n / len(yte)
    rows.append({"model": name, "test_auc": roc_auc_score(yte, p), "test_ap": average_precision_score(yte, p),
                 "precision@10%": hit / k, "churners_captured_%": 100 * hit / yte.sum(),
                 "campaign_value_cr": (hit * scale * save * value - k * scale * credit) / 1e7})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model").round(3))
print("Random call list precision:", round(yte.mean(), 3))

steps.title: Interpret with permutation importance
steps.detail: Permutation importance shuffles one input at a time on the test set and measures how much AUC drops: model-agnostic and computed on unseen data. Check that the top drivers make business sense (contract, complaints, tenure, call drops). If a feature you cannot act on or explain dominates, investigate before shipping.
steps.code:
imp = permutation_importance(best, Xte, yte, scoring="roc_auc", n_repeats=5, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1)
print(pd.Series(imp.importances_mean, index=features).sort_values(ascending=False).round(4))

steps.title: The leakage trap
steps.detail: Add `retention_call_logged` and rerun the logistic model in CV: AUC jumps towards 0.9+. It looks like a breakthrough but the field is only filled after the customer has already called to cancel, so it will not exist at prediction time. Ask of every feature: **would I know this value on the day I need the prediction?**
steps.code:
leaky = Pipeline([("pre", ColumnTransformer([("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("sc", StandardScaler())]), num + ["retention_call_logged"]),
                                              ("cat", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")), ("oh", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"))]), cat)])),
                  ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))])
leak_auc = cross_validate(leaky, train[features + ["retention_call_logged"]].astype({"retention_call_logged": int}), ytr, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc")["test_score"]
print(f"AUC with leaky feature: {leak_auc.mean():.3f}  vs honest logistic {table.loc['logistic', 'auc_mean']:.3f}")

deliverables: A CV comparison table (ROC AUC and PR AUC, mean ± SD) for the three pipelines on identical folds.
The tuned model's parameters and the paired per-fold comparison that justifies (or rejects) the extra complexity.
A test-set business table: precision@10%, share of churners captured and campaign ₹ value vs the logistic baseline.
A permutation-importance chart with a short interpretation, and a paragraph on the leakage trap and how you would prevent it in production.

rubric.good: One shared preprocessing block inside pipelines; same CV folds for all models; test set untouched until the end.
Reports fold SDs and paired differences; does not claim a winner from a difference inside the noise.
Randomized search on training data only with sensible ranges; realistic about gains.
Top-decile precision and ₹ value computed with the stated save rate, value and credit cost.
Identifies the leaky column, explains why it is unavailable at prediction time, quantifies the false gain.
Permutation importance on test data; drivers checked for business sense.

extensions: Add interaction features (complaints × monthly contract, call_drops > 3) to the logistic model and see how much of the gap to gradient boosting closes.
Use uplift thinking: simulate that the offer only works on customers with complaints, and compare ranking by churn risk vs by expected uplift.
Wrap the final pipeline with `CalibratedClassifierCV` and choose the call-list size that maximises expected ₹ value instead of a fixed 10%.
